transcript.answer: Only partly. Sending the token as the WebSocket subprotocol keeps it out of the URL and request line, so a URL-based access log won't capture it. It is still in the `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` request header, so any log, proxy or ingress that captures request headers can record it. The earlier claim that this avoids log exposure was 'only half true'. In the original design the server also echoed the token in the 101 response headers and held it on the socket object (`ws.protocol`), where a header-capturing ingress log, a proxy trace or a debug `console.log(ws)` could expose it. Issue #150 fixed that. Clients now offer `hal.v1, <token>` and the server answers only the `hal.v1` marker, so the token is in no response header and not on the socket object. The security docs were to be changed to stop claiming unqualified log protection and to name the remaining request-header exposure. Operators should redact `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` in request-header logging. No offered subprotocol value is to be written to any log, including in the close handler. This also means a subprotocol-carried token must be a valid HTTP token, so padded base64 can't be used.
sources: issue-150 (re-cinq/Otto #150: Stop echoing the access token in the WebSocket handshake response)

judgements.reason: The answer says it is not fully safe, explains that the server echoed the token into the 101 response headers where ingress/proxy logs can capture it, and describes the fix in which the client offers hal.v1 first and the server selects that marker.
